title: Bogle's Folly

beats.text: In nineteen seventy-six, a man launched a fund built to be average.
Imagine you're Jack Bogle. You hoped to raise a hundred and fifty million dollars.
The bankers bring in about eleven million.
You call it an abject failure.
The bankers offer to scrap it. You say no.
Critics call it Bogle's Folly. Rivals say nobody settles for average.
So why buy a fund that can't win?
You see, the market is one giant pizza every investor shares.
Before fees, the average slice is exactly the market. That's arithmetic.
But stock pickers take a bite first: salaries, research, trading.
Your fund takes a crumb, under half a percent a year.
So the average dollar chasing the market must trail it.
The folly was never being average. It was paying to try.

facts.claim: John C. Bogle launched First Index Investment Trust (now Vanguard 500 Index Fund), the first index mutual fund, on August 31, 1976
Bogle hoped the initial underwriting would raise up to $150 million (Vanguard/IFA: $50-150 million; Zweig/Evidence Investor: $150 million target)
The offering raised a little more than $11 million ($11.3 million)
Bogle himself called the result 'an abject failure'
The underwriters offered to scrap the launch / give the money back; Bogle refused
Critics called index funds un-American (Wall Street poster: 'Help Stamp Out Index Funds! Index Funds are Un-American')
Rival industry leader(s) said investors would not be satisfied with average returns
The fund launched with operating expenses of 0.43% a year (under half a percent)
Sharpe (FAJ 1991): before costs the average actively managed dollar earns the same as the average passive dollar (the market); after costs it must be less, for any period

caption:
1976: the first index mutual fund hoped for $150 million and raised about $11 million.
Critics called it Bogle's Folly, and un-American.
The arithmetic of fees said otherwise.
